topics.title: Surface observing (temperature, pressure, wind, visibility)
lesson: Surface observations are the base data for analysis, forecasts and verification. Standard exposure rules make observations comparable between stations.

list: Temperature and humidity: thermometer bulbs 1.25 to 2 m above ground level, in a white double-louvered screen (Stevenson screen) over short grass. The screen shields them from direct sunlight, precipitation and heat radiated from the ground, while letting air flow through.

Wind: wind measurements must be representative of winds 10 m above level terrain. METAR and SPECI report a two-minute mean. Direction is the direction the wind comes FROM, in degrees true to the nearest 10 (MANOBS 3.2.3), and instruments must work up to at least 100 kt. Siting: at least 10 times the height of any obstruction away.

Pressure: barometer. Station pressure is the pressure at the instrument. Mean sea level pressure (MSLP) is the station pressure reduced to sea level, so stations at different heights can be compared on a chart.

Visibility (aeronautical): the greater of (1) the greatest distance a black object near the ground can be easily recognized, and (2) the greatest distance lights of about 1,000 candela can be seen and identified against an unlit background. It is observed at eye level, 1.5 m above the ground. Canadian land stations report it in statute miles; if the observed value falls between two reportable values the lower one is reported, and 15 SM is the maximum reportable value.
Precipitation: rain gauges (tipping bucket or weighing), snow depth and water equivalent.

Cloud: observer estimates, or a laser ceilometer that measures cloud base height (AWOS ceilometers report cloud bases up to 25,000 ft). At airports, heights are measured from the official aerodrome level; elsewhere from ground level at the station.

QNH: sea level pressure setting. With QNH set, the altimeter reads aerodrome elevation when on the ground and altitude above mean sea level in flight. In North America this is the altimeter setting in inches of mercury (for example A2992).
QFE: setting that makes the altimeter read zero on the aerodrome.

Standard setting 29.92 inHg (1013.2 hPa): set after entering the standard pressure region, so all aircraft share one reference. In the altimeter setting region the station altimeter setting is used instead (Canadian Aviation Regulations, s. 602.37).

Reporting temperature and dew point (MANOBS 8.3): rounded to the nearest whole degree Celsius; a value ending in 0.5 rounds up to the warmer degree; single digits are written with a leading 0 (06); below 0 C the value is preceded by M (M02).
Pressure units (MANOBS 9.1.3): station and sea level pressure are in hPa; altimeter setting is in hundredths of inches of mercury.

Altimeter setting (MANOBS 9.2): QNH is rounded DOWN to the nearest hundredth of an inch of mercury and reported as four digits after the letter A. Sensors are accurate to within 0.02 inHg and aviation barometers have two or more independent sensors.

Sea level pressure (SLP) is reported as the last three digits of the hPa value including tenths. Remarks PRESRR or PRESFR are used when station pressure is rising or falling by 2.0 hPa per hour or more.

lesson.note: Automated stations report a limited set of elements. An LWIS reports only wind, altimeter setting, temperature and dew point. A METAR AUTO adds visibility, cloud height and coverage, precipitation and obstructions to vision. Systems outside lightning-detection coverage cannot report thunderstorms.

terms: Ventilated white box for housing thermometers.
Mean sea level pressure: station pressure reduced to sea level.
Altimeter setting that makes an altimeter read elevation above sea level.

questions.q: What is the standard height of an anemometer?
c: 10 m above open, level ground
2 m above the ground, as for the thermometer screen
30 m above the ground, as on a tower
On the roof of any nearby building

questions.q: Why are thermometers housed in a ventilated screen?
c: To shield them from sun and rain while allowing air flow
To keep them warm so readings stay above freezing at night
To make the readings equal to the temperature of the ground
To reduce wind speed so the thermometer is not blown over
questions.e: A Stevenson screen is a white double-louvered box. It shields thermometers from direct sunlight, precipitation and ground heat radiation while air flows through (MANCLIM).

c: The aerodrome elevation
Zero
The pressure altitude
The density altitude

c: Station pressure reduced to sea level
Pressure measured on a ship at sea only
The pressure at the 500 hPa level aloft
The average pressure of all stations in the region
questions.e: MSLP allows comparison of stations at different elevations.

c: Ceilometer
Psychrometer
Anemometer
Pyranometer
questions.e: A ceilometer uses a laser pulse and timing to measure cloud base height.

c: Direct sunlight, precipitation and ground reflection
Wind and pressure changes, while allowing sunlight to reach them
Humidity and wind, but it must be sealed from the air
Only wind and snow, leaving the sunlight to warm them
questions.e: The screen shields the thermometers from direct sunlight, precipitation and heat radiated from the ground, while air still flows through it (MANCLIM).

c: 10 m above ground
2 m above the ground, level with a standard thermometer
50 m above the ground, clear of nearby obstacles
1 m above the ground, in the middle of the screen
questions.e: MANOBS 3.2.2: wind measurements are representative of winds 10 m above level terrain.

questions.q: Wind direction is reported as the direction the wind is blowing:
c: From
To
Across
Around
questions.e: Wind direction is the direction the wind comes from, in degrees true (MANOBS 3.2.1 and 3.2.3).

questions.q: For aeronautical purposes, how does MANOBS define visibility?
c: The greater of the daytime distance a black object is recognized and the night distance lights are identified
The distance to the farthest cloud base that can be seen from the station, unless a supervisor directs otherwise
The average of the distances to the four nearest visibility markers
The distance at which a white object just blends into the background sky, based on the most recent routine report

questions.q: Barometric pressure is reduced to sea level to:
c: Allow comparison between stations at different elevations
Make the readings more accurate at each individual station
Remove the effect of temperature error in the barometer
Measure the wind speed at the surface more reliably
questions.e: Reduction removes the effect of station elevation.

questions.q: A ceilometer measures:
c: Cloud base height
Wind speed
Visibility only
Rainfall
questions.e: Laser or light pulses detect the cloud base.

questions.q: How is the altimeter setting rounded in a Canadian METAR?
c: Down to the nearest hundredth of an inch of mercury
Up to the nearest tenth of an inch of mercury, unless a supervisor directs otherwise
To the nearest whole hPa, with no decimals, unless a supervisor directs otherwise
To the nearest 0.5 inHg on the dial
questions.e: MANOBS 9.2: QNH is rounded down to the nearest whole hundredth of an inch of mercury.

questions.q: An observed temperature of 4.5 C is reported as:
questions.e: MANOBS 8.3: values involving 0.5 C round up to the warmer degree, and single digits take a leading 0.

c: PRESFR
PRESRR
PRESFAL
LOWPRES

c: At least 10 times the height of the obstruction
At least twice the height of the obstruction
At least 100 m regardless of the obstruction's height
Directly beside it, for shelter from the wind
questions.e: MANOBS 3.2.2: representative of winds 10 m above level terrain at a distance equal to at least 10 times the height of any object from that object.

c: 10 degrees
1 degree
5 degrees
45 degrees

topics.title: Upper-air soundings and radiosondes
lesson: Upper-air soundings measure the atmosphere above ground. Almost all of the world's upper-air data comes from radiosondes: small instrument packages carried aloft by a hydrogen or helium balloon.

list: Standard launch times are 00 and 12 UTC. This gives models and forecasters a simultaneous snapshot of the atmosphere.
A radiosonde measures pressure, temperature and humidity. Wind is derived by tracking the balloon's position, now usually by GPS.

The balloon expands as the pressure falls and eventually bursts, then the instrument parachutes back. NOAA says sondes can reach over 115,000 ft (about 35 km) and flights can last more than two hours.
Data are reported at mandatory pressure levels (for example 1000, 925, 850, 700, 500, 400, 300, 250, 200, 150, 100 hPa) plus significant levels where the profile changes.
Plot on a skew-T log-P to assess stability, cloud layers, freezing level and inversions.
Initialize and verify numerical weather prediction models.
Determine winds aloft and jet streams.
Calibrate and cross-check satellite measurements.

lesson: Stations are far apart (hundreds of km) and launch only twice a day, so small features such as thunderstorm outflows are missed. Balloons drift downwind, and the profile is not strictly vertical.

lesson.note: Aircraft reports (AMDAR), wind profilers and satellite retrievals fill gaps between launches.

terms: Instrument package carried by balloon that transmits profiles of pressure, temperature, humidity and wind.
Standard pressure level at which every sounding reports data.
Level where the profile changes character, reported in addition to mandatory levels.

questions.q: At which times are routine radiosonde launches made?
c: 00 and 12 UTC
06 and 18 UTC only
Every hour
Only when storms approach
questions.e: NOAA: most upper-air observations are taken daily at 00Z and 12Z.

questions.q: Which variables does a radiosonde provide?
c: Pressure, temperature, humidity and wind
Temperature and wind only, without humidity
Cloud height, visibility and precipitation type
Radar reflectivity and lightning strike counts
questions.e: A radiosonde measures pressure, temperature and humidity, and wind is derived from tracking.

questions.q: Why does the balloon eventually burst?
c: It expands as outside pressure drops until it ruptures
Its gas freezes solid in the cold air near the tropopause
It is struck by lightning inside high thunderstorm cloud
The gas leaks out gradually and the balloon cannot rise higher
questions.e: The gas expands at lower pressure until the balloon reaches its limit.

questions.q: Which of these are standard (mandatory) pressure levels?
c: 850 and 500 hPa
875 and 525 hPa
950 and 450 hPa
1100 and 20 hPa
questions.e: 850 and 500 hPa are among the standard mandatory levels.

questions.q: What is a major limitation of radiosonde coverage?
c: Stations are widely spaced and launch only twice a day
They can measure surface values only and not the upper air
They are launched only over water and not over land
They cannot measure temperature in clear air or in cloud
questions.e: Small, fast-evolving features can occur between stations and launch times.

questions.q: A radiosonde is carried aloft by:
c: A balloon
An aircraft
A rocket
A satellite
questions.e: Weather balloons lift the instrument package.

questions.q: Radiosondes are normally released at:
c: 00 and 12 UTC
06 and 18 local only
Noon only
Every hour
questions.e: NOAA: most upper-air observations are taken daily at 00Z and 12Z.

questions.q: A radiosonde measures:
c: Pressure, temperature and humidity, with wind from tracking
Rainfall and snowfall only, with wind from the ground station
Visibility and cloud base only, from a laser on the balloon
Lightning strikes and ozone, with wind taken from the ground
questions.e: Wind is derived from tracking the balloon.

questions.q: A balloon bursts at about:
c: 30 km or higher
3 km, where the air is too thin for the balloon to float
1 km, once the first cloud layer is reached
About 100 m, where the surface inversion ends
questions.e: NOAA: sondes can reach over 115,000 ft (about 35 km). The balloon bursts as it expands in the thin air.

questions.q: Why are upper-air observations important for forecasting?
c: They provide initial conditions for models and stability data
They measure the ground temperature at each station only
They only support the military and have no use for models
They measure visibility and cloud for the next hour only
questions.e: Soundings give the vertical structure used in analyses.

questions.q: How is the wind measured by a modern radiosonde?
c: By tracking the position of the sonde with GPS
By a cup anemometer carried on the balloon
By the balloon's rate of rise alone
By a separate aircraft flying alongside the balloon
questions.e: NOAA: wind speed and direction are derived by tracking the sonde's position with GPS.

topics.title: Weather radar principles and interpretation
lesson: A weather radar sends out short pulses of microwave energy and listens for the part scattered back by raindrops, snow, hail and other particles. Time delay gives range. Signal strength gives reflectivity.

Reflectivity (Z) is measured in mm6/m3. Because raw values vary so widely, radar applies a logarithmic scale, giving dBZ. The scale runs from about -35 to +85 dBZ. Higher values mean more or larger targets. ECCC public radar maps show precipitation rate instead: mm/h for rain and cm/h for snow.

list: NOAA JetStream guide (US, not ECCC): above 65 dBZ extremely heavy precipitation including water-coated hail. 50 to 65: heavy precipitation, possibly some hail. 40 to 50: moderate. 20 to 40: light. 0 to 20: very light precipitation or general clutter. -35 to 0: extremely light (drizzle or snow).

NOAA marks the 20 to 40 and 40 to 50 rows as general guidelines: heavy rainfall does not always match them. Warm tropical rain contains little or no hail, so reflectivity is often lower than the rain rate suggests.

lesson: Doppler radar measures the radial velocity: the part of the target motion toward or away from the radar. It cannot see motion across the beam. A tight pair of strong inbound and outbound velocities next to each other suggests rotation, such as a mesocyclone.

Dual-pol radars send and receive both horizontal and vertical pulses. ECCC says its S-band dual-pol radars help distinguish precipitation types, reduce false echoes from birds and insects, improve quantitative precipitation estimates and help detect icing conditions for aircraft. ECCC's surface precipitation type product classifies rain, snow, freezing rain, hail and mixed.

list: Differential reflectivity (ZDR, dB): compares horizontal and vertical power. Near 0 dB suggests round or tumbling targets such as hail. Above 0 suggests flattened drops such as large raindrops. Below 0 suggests vertically elongated particles such as ice crystals or snowflakes (NOAA).

Correlation coefficient (CC, 0 to 1): how similar the sampled targets are. Low is below 0.80, moderate 0.80 to 0.97, high above 0.97. Birds, insects, buildings, smoke and mixed precipitation give lower CC than uniform rain or snow (NOAA).

Tornado debris signature: a significant drop in CC at the same place as a strong rotational velocity couplet. Debris must be lofted high enough to be sampled, so no CC drop does not rule a tornado out (NOAA).

Beam height rises with range. NOAA examples: about 1,300 ft above ground at 20 miles and about 11,600 ft at 98 miles for the radars cited. The beam also widens by about 1,000 ft per 10 miles, nearly 2 miles wide at 100 miles. Distant low-level precipitation can be overshot.
Subrefraction: the beam bends less than normal, so the radar overshoots objects it would normally detect and may under-report intensity.

Superrefraction: the beam is closer to the ground than normal and storm intensity can be overestimated. Extreme superrefraction causes ducting and false echoes called anomalous propagation (AP), for example roads or railways showing up on the display.
Ground clutter: stationary echoes near the radar from terrain and buildings.
Bright band: melting snowflakes appear as a ring of high reflectivity at the melting level, overestimating rain rate.
Attenuation: heavy rain can weaken the signal, especially for shorter wavelengths.

lesson.h: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (radar page)

list: Radar helps identify areas of precipitation. It does not show cloud cover. Pilots unfamiliar with radar products are advised to contact an FIC for NAV CANADA assistance.
Imagery comes in two formats: a precipitation intensity product and an echo tops product.
Precipitation intensity is a rate of fall in mm/h or cm/h at a specific altitude (example given: 1.5 km). Two scales: rain up to 300 mm/h, snow up to 40 cm/h.
Echo tops give an indication of the vertical extent of the precipitation area. Cloud tops could extend much higher.

Each radar site has a detection range of about 150 NM. Composites join several radar images into one; their advantage is that anomalies such as attenuation and masking are reduced, because adjacent sites see the precipitation from other directions.
The guide's network map (MSC's Weather Radar Network) shows 32 operational radars. Composite and single-site images are available in colour on the CFPS website.

Older C-band radars are being replaced by more powerful S-band dual-pol radars (Canadian Weather Radar Replacement Program, launched 2017). C-band: single polarization, Doppler coverage 113 km, maximum coverage 256 km, new product every 10 minutes, 24 scans. S-band: dual polarization, Doppler coverage 240 km, maximum 330 km (raw data only), every 6 minutes, 17 scans.
The precipitation-rate mosaic covers Canada and the US at 1 km resolution, updates every 6 minutes and can merge up to 200 radars. Palettes come in 8 or 14 colours.

DPQPE (dual-pol quantitative precipitation estimate) uses the lowest sweep, 0.4 degrees for most S-band radars. SPTP (surface precipitation type) has five classes: rain, snow, freezing rain, hail, mixed.

ECCC cautions: do not compare intensity and SPTP pixel by pixel; the intensity composite uses a maximum-value approach where radars overlap; interpolated values should not be treated as real observations; SPTP uses only the nearest radar plus model data, so some echoes may be removed.

lesson.note: Always check beam height at distance before trusting low-level echoes.

terms: Component of motion toward or away from the radar.
Enhanced reflectivity at the melting layer.
Radar beam bent toward the ground, producing false echoes.
Differential reflectivity: power comparison between horizontal and vertical channels, in dB.
Unitless 0 to 1 measure of how similar the sampled targets are.

questions.q: What does a Doppler radar measure that a conventional radar does not?
c: Radial velocity
Cloud colour
Temperature
Air pressure
questions.e: Doppler radars detect motion toward or away from the radar.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, what reflectivity is usually associated with heavy rain and possible hail?
c: About 50 to 65 dBZ, extremely heavy above 65
Below 10 dBZ, which is only drizzle or haze
Around 20 dBZ, which is light rain at most
Zero dBZ, which means no echo at all
questions.e: NOAA JetStream table (US guidance): 50 to 65 heavy, possibly some hail; above 65 extremely heavy including water-coated hail. ECCC public maps use rain rate.

questions.q: Why might a radar miss shallow precipitation at long range?
c: The beam rises above it due to Earth's curvature
Rain evaporates completely before the beam reaches it
The radar signal is absorbed by dry air at long range
Distant echoes are too bright and saturate the receiver
questions.e: The beam height increases with distance and can overshoot low clouds and rain.

questions.q: What is the radar 'bright band'?
c: A ring of enhanced reflectivity at the melting level
A band of heavy snow falling at the edge of the beam
A thunderstorm signature shown at the radar's maximum range
A false echo created by ground clutter near the radar
questions.e: Melting snowflakes are coated in water and reflect strongly.

questions.q: What is a main benefit of dual-polarization radar?
c: It helps identify precipitation type and non-weather targets
It extends the range of the radar to well over 1000 km
It measures lightning strikes inside the radar coverage area
It gives the surface air temperature under each radar echo
questions.e: Dual-pol variables give particle shape and type information.

questions.q: Radar reflectivity is expressed in:
c: dBZ
hPa
kt
mm
questions.e: dBZ is a logarithmic measure of returned power.

questions.q: The Doppler effect allows radar to measure:
c: Radial velocity toward or away from the radar
Temperature and humidity along the beam path from the antenna
Pressure and cloud type in the sample volume
Cloud colour and drop size distribution of the echo
questions.e: Frequency shift gives motion along the beam.

questions.q: Ground clutter appears as:
c: Stationary echoes near the radar
Moving bands that travel with the wind across the display
Hook shapes on the edge of a rotating storm cell
Clear air patterns that appear on calm, clear days
questions.e: Terrain and buildings return signals.

questions.q: The radar beam rises with distance because of:
c: Earth's curvature and beam elevation
Wind blowing the beam upward as it travels away
Cloud layers refracting the beam toward the sky
Temperature of the air at the radar antenna only
questions.e: The beam rises above the ground as it travels.

questions.q: Bright band on radar marks:
c: The melting layer
Hail
Ground clutter
Birds
questions.e: Melting snow coats with water and gives high reflectivity.

questions.q: Higher dBZ values generally indicate:
c: Heavier precipitation or larger hydrometeors
Lighter precipitation or smaller drops in the beam
No precipitation, since the echo is only clutter
Only snow, since rain always gives a low reading
questions.e: Stronger returns mean larger or more numerous targets.

questions.q: Approximately what range does the dBZ scale cover?
c: -35 to +85 dBZ
0 to 20 dBZ
0 to 1000 dBZ
-5 to +10 dBZ
questions.e: NOAA JetStream, Radar Images: Reflectivity.

c: Light precipitation
Moderate precipitation
Heavy precipitation
Hail only

Flattened, such as large raindrops
Vertically elongated, such as snowflakes
Non-existent

c: Non-meteorological echoes or mixed precipitation
Uniform light rain falling over the whole area

Clear air with no echoes of any kind

A radar blind spot behind a hill

About 10 ft

topics.title: Satellite imagery (visible, IR, water vapour)
lesson: Satellites provide global coverage, including oceans where there are few surface observations.

list: Geostationary: about 35,786 km (22,236 mi) above the equator, fixed over one spot. Frequent images of the same region. Poor viewing at high latitudes. The GOES satellites are geostationary.

Polar-orbiting: about 833 km up per NOAA; the NAV CANADA guide says about 850 km for POES satellites with HRPT (High-Resolution Picture Transfer), one orbit every 105 minutes, 14 orbits a day. Because the Earth rotates, each orbit shifts west by about 2 time zones. Higher resolution and good polar coverage, but fewer passes of a given spot.

Visible: reflected sunlight, daytime only. Clouds appear white, the ground grey and water dark. Snow-covered ground also looks white and can be mistaken for cloud or fog; looping helps because clouds move and snow does not. Visible can show low fog and stratus that IR misses, if higher cloud does not cover them. It shows developing thunderstorms in their earliest stages, before radar detects them (NWS).

Infrared (IR): heat radiated by clouds and the surface. Day and night. Clouds are colder than land and water, so they stand out. Strong to severe thunderstorms normally have very cold tops. Colder temperatures are often enhanced with colours. Low stratus and fog are often hard to identify in IR.

Water vapour: moisture in the upper atmosphere. Brightest or whitest areas are the most humid and dark areas are dry. Looped imagery shows jet streams and upper troughs even in clear areas, and a stream of water vapour crossing a mountain range at a near right angle may indicate mountain wave turbulence (NWS).

GOES water vapour bands: 6.2 micrometres (upper level), 6.9 (mid level), 7.3 (lower level, senses down to about 500 to 750 hPa in cloud-free areas). Each senses the mean temperature of a layer of moisture; layer height varies with the temperature and moisture profile. Optically dense cloud blocks the view of lower moisture.

lesson.h: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (satellite page)

list: Visible and infrared imagery are the two most common types on the CFPS website, from geostationary or polar-orbiting satellites. The guide's example is a GOES-East IR (C13) image dated 2026-05-15, with a temperature scale in degrees C.
Visible: a photo of the clouds during daylight hours. Infrared: measures the heat (thermal) footprint of cloud or of the Earth's surface if clouds are thin or absent, day and night.
GOES: about 36,000 km above the equator, position fixed relative to a point on the surface.
Owing to the complexity of interpreting satellite imagery, most pilots should consider consulting a briefer when using satellite products for flight planning.
Very cold, bright cloud tops fit strong to severe thunderstorms. A textured anvil is a common deep-convection sign (anvil appearance not confirmed in the sources used).
A comma-shaped cloud pattern marks a developing mid-latitude cyclone (standard practice, not confirmed in the sources used).

Low cloud and fog are hard to separate from the ground in IR because they are close to surface temperature. Compare visible and IR, or use the night fog product, which combines two IR channels and shows fog and low cloud as dark areas.
NAV CANADA advises most pilots to consult a briefer before using satellite products for flight planning.

lesson.note: Visible shows reflected sunlight (daytime only). IR shows radiated heat, so cloud-top temperature, day and night. Water vapour shows upper-level moisture.

terms: Orbit that keeps a satellite over a fixed point on the equator.
Temperature a blackbody would have to emit the observed IR radiance.
Dark wedge of dry air in water vapour imagery wrapping into a cyclone.

topics.title: Reading and plotting a skew-T log-P
lesson: A skew-T log-P diagram plots a sounding. Pressure is the vertical axis on a log scale. Isotherms are skewed to the right at about 45 degrees. Three families of reference lines are drawn on it.

list: Isotherms: lines of constant temperature, sloping up to the right.
Dry adiabats: curved lines sloping up to the left. A lifted unsaturated parcel follows these.
Moist (saturated) adiabats: curved lines that lean toward the dry adiabats at high levels. Saturated parcels follow these.
Mixing ratio lines: dashed lines that slope up to the right.
Temperature (right line) and dew point (left line) profiles. When they are close or touch, the layer is moist or in cloud. A wide spread means dry air.
Inversion: temperature increases with height (the line moves right as you go up).
Freezing level: where the temperature line crosses 0 C.
Wind barbs along the side give winds aloft.
Lifted condensation level (LCL): lift a surface parcel along its dry adiabat and its mixing ratio line from the dew point. They meet at the LCL.
Level of free convection (LFC): where the lifted parcel becomes warmer than the environment. Equilibrium level (EL): where it is again equal to the environment, near the expected cloud top.
CAPE: area between the parcel path and the environment where the parcel is warmer. More area means stronger updrafts.
CIN: area where the parcel is colder. A cap that inhibits convection.
Lifted index (LI): environment temperature at 500 hPa minus parcel temperature at 500 hPa. Negative values mean unstable.

lesson.note: Quick read: dew point near temperature means moisture. Temperature crossing back to the right means an inversion. Large positive area means storms if lift exists.

terms: Positive area on a sounding between the parcel curve and environment.
Convective inhibition: negative area that must be overcome for convection.

questions.q: On a skew-T, CAPE is represented by:
c: The area where the lifted parcel is warmer than the environment
The area where the lifted parcel is colder than the environment
The distance between T and Td at the surface
The slope of the isotherms on the diagram
questions.e: CAPE is the positive buoyancy area between the parcel path and environment curve.

questions.q: If the dew point line is very close to the temperature line over a layer, that layer is:
c: Moist or in cloud
Very dry
An inversion
Unrelated to moisture
questions.e: A small spread means near-saturation.

Where the isotherm through the surface dew point meets the moist adiabat at 500 hPa, unless a supervisor directs otherwise
Where the temperature line first crosses the 0 C isotherm above the surface
At the pressure level where the dew point line reaches the left edge of the chart, under normal operating conditions
questions.e: A lifted unsaturated parcel saturates where those two lines intersect.

questions.q: A negative lifted index indicates:
c: Unstable conditions
Stable conditions
No moisture
A strong inversion
questions.e: A negative LI means the parcel is warmer than its environment at 500 hPa.

questions.q: How does an inversion appear on a skew-T?
c: The temperature line shifts to the right with increasing height
The temperature line follows a dry adiabat to the left with height
The dew point line crosses to the right of the temperature line
The temperature line is exactly vertical from the surface to 500 hPa
questions.e: Temperature increasing with height makes the profile lean back toward higher temperatures.

questions.q: On a skew-T, isotherms are drawn:
c: Slanting from lower left to upper right
Vertically, from the bottom of the chart to the top
Horizontally, from the left side to the right side
As curved lines that follow the moist adiabats upward
questions.e: The skew gives the diagram its name.

questions.q: The dewpoint curve lying close to the temperature curve indicates:
c: Moist, near saturated layers
Very dry air with a large temperature-dew point spread
A strong inversion capping a layer of warm air
A cold front passing through the sounding level
questions.e: Small spread means near saturation.

questions.q: The LCL on a skew-T is found where:
c: Dry adiabat from the surface temperature meets the mixing ratio line from the dew point
Where two isotherms cross on the chart at the surface
Where the dry adiabat from the surface meets the freezing level, under normal operating conditions
Where the isobars cross the surface temperature line on the chart, as set out in the governing publication
questions.e: Lifted parcel reaches saturation at that intersection.

questions.q: An area of positive buoyancy on a skew-T lies:
c: Between the parcel curve and the environment, parcel warmer
Where the parcel curve is colder than the environment curve
Below the surface, between the two isotherm lines
Between two isotherms drawn at the same pressure
questions.e: Positive area gives CAPE.

questions.q: An inversion on a skew-T appears as:
c: A section where temperature increases with height
A vertical line where temperature does not change with height
A steep drop in temperature with height at the surface
A closed loop on the right side of the diagram
questions.e: The temperature curve leans right with height.

questions.q: A sounding with temperature below 0 C through a deep layer and warm layer above indicates:
c: Potential for freezing rain or ice pellets
Hot, dry weather with a deep well-mixed boundary layer
Fog only, with no precipitation and a shallow stable layer
Nothing useful, since the temperature curve is not significant
questions.e: Warm nose aloft over sub-zero surface layer.
